name: Dolores Pruitt
equipment: .38 revolver, Smith & Wesson Model 10, her retired-officer carry permit gun (6 loaded)
Expandable baton, which she has not opened in anger since 2009
Retired Merriwick Transit Police shield in a cracked leather wallet
A transit 'drop key' that opens every platform-end gate and track-access door in the Under, which she was supposed to hand in and did not
Heavy rubber flashlight (the kind that is also a club)
Reading glasses on a chain, and a second pair in her coat because she loses the first
A folded paper subway map from 1998 annotated in four colours of pen
MetroCard with eleven dollars left on it, now worthless
features: Human (+1 to all six ability scores)
Combat Training: Marksman (+2 to ranged attack rolls; already included in her revolver's attack bonus)
Adrenaline (bonus action: regain 1d10+1 hit points, once per short rest)
Weapon proficiencies: Melee, Sidearms, Longarms, Automatics, Explosives, Energy Weapons
Cop Contacts (Police Officer feature: serving and retired transit and city police recognise her, will share what they know and extend her a professional courtesy)

personality.traits: I count exits when I walk into a room, and I count heads when I walk out of one. I talk to frightened people the way I talked to them on a stalled train for thirty-one years: slow, low, and as if this happens every Thursday.
personality.ideals: Nobody gets left on the platform. You walk the whole train before you call it clear, every car, every time.
personality.bonds: My grandson Desmond, who is twelve, who goes to Gansevoort Middle School up in Harlow, and who I was supposed to pick up at five.
personality.flaws: I have a gun and I was trained to use it, and I keep reaching for it in a city where the loudest thing in the street is the thing that gets taken. I also do not ask for help, and I am sixty-three, and my knees know it.

appearance: A short, solid Black woman of sixty-three in a long navy wool car coat, sensible shoes and a grey crop of hair she cuts herself. Reading glasses on a chain. She stands with her weight back on her heels like someone used to a moving floor, and she has a transit cop's habit of looking at people's hands before their faces. Her voice carries without being raised, which was the single most useful thing she owned for thirty-one years.
backstory: Dolores Pruitt rode the Merriwick Under for thirty-one years as a Transit Police officer and retired a sergeant out of District 4, which is Union Terminal and everything under it. She has walked every tunnel in the Meridian with a flashlight, talked a man down off the Harrow Street platform edge on her fortieth birthday, and delivered one baby on a stalled Red Line train between 51st and 59th. She retired at sixty, tried Florida for a winter and hated it, and came home to a rent-controlled one-bedroom on Sixty-Eighth and a life of picking her grandson up from school three days a week. At 4:12 on the Thursday she is in the Union Terminal concourse with a coffee, waiting for the 4:30 Green Line uptown, when the light changes, every phone in the hall plays the same tone at once, and the floor she has stood on all her working life stops feeling like it belongs to anyone. Her first thought is the boy. Her second, which arrives about half a second later and which she is a little ashamed of, is that there are four hundred people in this hall and she is the only one in it who has done this before.
